bollymeter.basis: 69% from 36 critics on Rotten Tomatoes. Audiences responded far more warmly at 94%, suggesting the show's pulpy action-fantasy DNA connected with viewers the critical consensus undervalued. The fight choreography and Alba Baptista's performance were consistent praise points.

seasons.review_body: Warrior Nun debuted on Netflix in July 2020, adapted from Ben Dunn's comic by showrunner Simon Barry and filmed largely in Spain. The premise - a paralysed young woman resurrected by a holy artefact that bonds to her spine, forcing her into a secret Catholic warrior order - sounds maximalist, and in Season 1 the show sometimes struggles to balance its mythology-building with its character work. Critics landed at 69 percent from 36 reviews, with reservations centring on heavy-handed setup and world-construction that occasionally stalls the pace. The audience found the same material considerably more compelling - 94 percent on Rotten Tomatoes with over 2,500 ratings - pointing to the show's genuine strength: Alba Baptista's performance as Ava Silva, the fight choreography filmed in Spanish architecture, and a sincerity about its genre premise that the algorithm-era rarely allows. Season 1 is the rougher half of the show's run, but it plants the foundations the second season would build on.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Warrior Nun S1E1: "Psalm 46:5" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

Ava begins with death as a wish, a brutal place for any show to start. she says she spent her whole life dreaming about being dead, and the hour takes that thought literally enough to make it dangerous. Elsewhere, nuns speak in the language of devils, shrapnel, protocol, and sacrifice. A wounded **Shannon** needs time. **Ava** gets life. The trade is not explained cleanly because the episode is built around that mess: a resurrection that feels less like salvation than a problem nobody signed for.

## Death Gets the First Word

"Psalm 46:5" works best when resurrection interrupts rather than parades as a miracle. Ava does not wake into wonder. She wakes into contradiction. Her early voice frames death as something she has imagined, even wanted, and then the plot answers with the ugliest possible joke. Life returns without consent, context, or instructions.

BollyAI's read: the hour's central claim is that being chosen can look a lot like being trapped. The show has ready-made mythology in its religious language, with talk of the Devil presenting a pleasing visage and the sisters reading events through spiritual threat. Ava's side keeps dragging that mythology back down to the body. She walks. She tests. She asks what happened. Her reaction after realizing this is not a dream, "This is hardcore real life," lands because the line refuses holy polish.

That bluntness is the opener's cleanest tonal weapon. The show wants grandeur, but Ava keeps puncturing it with disbelief. The danger is that the dialogue has to carry a lot of setup, and the early stretch sometimes feels like everyone is pushing furniture into place before the real scene can begin. Still, the premise has bite: a girl who dreamed of death is forced to negotiate life as evidence.

## The Body Becomes the Mystery

The episode introduces its supernatural mechanics through emergency, which is the right choice. Before the audience gets a comfortable explanation, the sisters are dealing with Divinium shrapnel and the threat that it must be removed before it kills Shannon. That detail gives the fantasy a physical cost. No soft light. No vague destiny. Metal, injury, procedure, and a clock.

The opening injury sequence is dense with short exchanges, and that density helps. The room feels pressured. Orders come fast. Explanations arrive in pieces. Shannon says she will buy time because she is needed elsewhere, and the line turns sacrifice into logistics. That is sharper than a speech. She does not have the luxury of making her pain ceremonial.

The hour also plants its biggest mechanism without pretending it is solved: the Halo can do something nobody is ready to define. The open question of whether it has ever brought someone back gives the episode a working engine. The resurrection becomes a case file.

The writing wobbles when verbal scaffolding takes over. The show names its materials, dangers, spiritual frame, and institutional panic in quick succession. The result is solid world-building with visible seams. The hour earns attention, but it sometimes asks dialogue to do the work of dread.

## Mary Turns Grief Into Procedure

**Mary** is the hour's most useful pressure point because she treats chaos like a checklist. Her stated drive is survival: keep Shannon alive, make the team follow medical and protocol steps, account for what went wrong. Later, she gives the recovery-mission account and reports that Shannon was critically wounded by Divinium mixed with explosives. In another show, that would be exposition wearing boots. Here, it becomes character because Mary sounds like someone trying to control grief by filing it correctly.

That tension gives the episode some of its best texture. Mary wants the injury handled as a protocol problem, yet the way she speaks carries the weight of mission necessity and fatal risk. She talks as if this can be contained in an incident report, while the facts keep escaping the report. Shannon is injured. The system around her is cracking.

The show is smart to keep Mary near the practical horror of the situation rather than treating her as a pure emotional witness. She orders, explains, and accounts. That makes the grief harder because she has no room to perform it. The hour understands something useful about crisis scenes: the person giving instructions may be the person closest to falling apart.

Mary's material also exposes the episode's habit of over-explaining. Her recovery account has to deliver plot, stakes, and institutional memory in a compact space. The performance of control is compelling. The mechanics around it could use more silence.

## Ava Tests the Miracle Like a Fuse

Ava's arc moves from impossible event to practical experiment. She wants to understand why she is alive again, and she does it by testing what is possible and asking what is happening to her. That is the right instinct for a protagonist dropped into mythology. She does not accept the halo of the premise. She pokes it.

The midsection shifts from the clipped urgency of Shannon's injury to longer reflective and argumentative lines around Ava's disbelief-to-acceptance transition. That shift is necessary, but it is also where the pacing gets clumsier. Ava has to process a resurrection, the show has to explain the rules, and the hour has to keep its mystery alive without becoming coy. It mostly manages the balance because Ava's confusion is concrete. She is not asking abstract destiny questions. She is asking why her body is moving.

The final beat of someone seeing Ava walk and responding that she died works because it gives the premise a witness. Until that moment, resurrection can live inside Ava's confusion and the institution's panic. Once another person names the contradiction, the show locks its hook into place. Ava is a walking violation of the facts.

That is where the episode earns its season-opener function. It plants the questions cleanly: who or what resurrected Ava, what the Halo does, whether removing it will kill her, and what Shannon's absence means when someone expected family or friends and found none. The mystery board is full, but the strongest piece remains Ava's body.

## Father Vincent Wants the Story to Behave

**Father Vincent** enters as a figure of inquiry and control. He wants answers and trustworthy handling of the Halo situation, and he pushes for explanations. In an episode crowded with emergency language, that role matters. He gives the mythology an administrative face. The sacred object has to be managed, explained, protected, and possibly removed.

That angle keeps the show from floating into vague prophecy. The Halo becomes a problem of custody as much as faith. If removing it may kill Ava, then every spiritual decision has a medical and moral consequence. The episode does not need to resolve that dilemma yet. It only needs to make the question feel poisonous, and it does.

The weakness is that Father Vincent's scenes lean toward explanation more than conflict. He pushes for information, but the hour's spark still sits with Ava's disbelief and Mary's procedural grief. Vincent is valuable because he organizes the stakes. He is less vivid than the people bleeding under them.

That imbalance is manageable for a first chapter. It gives the series architecture. But the episode is livelier when characters discover the rules under pressure instead of discussing them as institutional concern.

## The Verdict

"Psalm 46:5" is a sturdy, intriguing opener with a sharp contradiction at its center: Ava wanted death, and life comes back as a demand. The hour is strongest when it lets that contradiction stay physical, through walking, injury, Divinium, and the brutal possibility that the Halo saves by endangering. It is weaker when exposition crowds the frame, especially when mythology, protocol, and backstory arrive in heavy traffic.

BollyAI's score: 7.2/10. The episode is solid but uneven, with a premise sharp enough to cut through its setup burden. As a season opener, it plants clean open loops around Ava's resurrection, Shannon's injury, the Halo's rules, and the cost of removing it. The best reason to continue is Ava realizing life has returned without asking her permission.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp resurrection hook powers a busy opener where Ava’s unwanted second life outclasses the exposition around it.

episode_reviews.title: Revelation 2:10
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season finale escalates the mythology beyond what the first run fully prepared for, but Baptista carries the emotional weight. The cliffhanger sets up a more confident Season 2.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final confrontation recontextualises who the show's true antagonist has always been.

bollymeter.basis: 100% on Rotten Tomatoes from 11 critics in Season 2 - a dramatic correction from Season 1's 69%. Reviewers consistently cited the bisexual romance arc, the science-fiction integration with religious mythology, and Baptista's grown performance as the season's defining improvements.

pull_quotes.text: Excellent action-adventure TV, with complex and nuanced women leads, and a bisexual love story anchoring the whole thing in place.
Season 2 is where things really kick into a new gear, fully blending science fiction and religion in a way I was not expecting.
A shining beacon of excellent romance, world-building, and commentary on our world that doesn't lag in its sophomore season.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 of Warrior Nun arrived in November 2022 and critics responded to a markedly more confident show - 100 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 11 reviews, a result that reflected both genuine improvement and the self-selecting nature of a smaller critical pool covering a cancelled series' final run. The show's central romance between Ava and Sister Beatrice (Kristina Tonteri-Young) developed into what multiple reviewers described as the season's emotional spine. Simon Barry's writing blended the series' science-fiction mythology more fluidly with its religious architecture, and the result felt like the show the first season was trying to become. Netflix cancelled Warrior Nun weeks after the season landed, citing viewing metrics - a decision that generated one of the more sustained fan campaigns in recent streaming history. Season 2 stands as the definitive version of the show: cleaner, bolder, and operating at a level the first season only periodically reached.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 fully integrates the science-fiction and religious mythology threads Season 1 kept separate, and the central romance moves from subtext to the load-bearing emotional structure.
